about: Engine E0 (the Site Bench, SB0; capstone C0; lesson A8 next): one site behind one meter, sized and run hour by hour as a linear program. Two fictional sites: a Prairie Town home and the ridge wind farm. Hourly shapes are Prairie Town's real 2025 shapes from the Southwest Power Pool grid (town_year.json, EIA-930). The home's household use, its heating need and its temperature are illustrative. Every cost is in 2025 dollars: a value from a source in another dollar year is converted with EIA's GDP price index (deflator below), and the engine does the conversion so that the test can check it. Costs are constant over the whole horizon (no change over time). No tax credits, incentives, taxes or financing charges are counted.

deflator.note: GDP implicit price deflator (index, 2017 = 100), the mean of EIA's monthly values for each year. A 2022 dollar is 1.093 2025 dollars.

finance.note: 4% real discount rate, as in lessons 7 and 13 (a round value inside the 2025 ATB's financing range). Money is in real 2025 dollars, so the rate is a real rate.

home.label: Prairie Town home

use.note: Illustrative: 9,000 kWh a year of household use (lights, appliances, cooling), following Prairie Town's hourly demand shape (SPP 2025). A real home's use is spikier than a whole grid's.

heat.note: Illustrative: 14,000 kWh of heat a year, in proportion to how far a smooth made-up temperature falls below 16 °C. The temperature is coldest on 15 January and at 03:00; real weather is lumpier, with cold snaps this year does not have.

solar.note: Rooftop panels follow SPP's 2025 solar shape, month by month (EIA's 2025 monthly capacity factors), scaled to a 17.6% yearly capacity factor, EIA's figure for a typical home system.

tariff.note: Illustrative: a flat 14¢/kWh, close to what Kansas homes paid on average in January to August 2025 (14.27¢/kWh). The time-of-use tariff charges three times as much from 16:00 to 21:00 (standard time, every day), set so that the household's use alone costs the same on either tariff (as in lesson A4).

export.note: Illustrative: the utility pays 4¢ for each kWh the panels send to the grid (net billing). Only the panels export; the battery does not.

grid.note: One yearly average for every hour: Kansas power plants emitted 680 lb of CO2 per MWh generated in 2024 (operating emissions; location-based). The bench counts the electricity bought minus the electricity sent back at this factor. An hourly or marginal factor would differ (case file CF6).

gas.note: The home's present gas furnace: 80% efficient (the minimum furnace in EIA's table). Gas at $14.81 per thousand cubic feet, what Kansas homes paid in 2025, with 1,036 Btu per cubic foot; 52.91 kg of CO2 per MMBtu burned.

pv.note: Installed cost $4,336 per kW (DC) in 2022 dollars, EIA's residential system; 25-year life. Upkeep of $20 per kW a year is illustrative.

battery.note: Illustrative installed cost of $1,000 per kWh (a home battery costs far more per kWh than the utility-scale batteries of lesson 13). Power = energy ÷ 2.5 hours, 85% round trip, fixed upkeep 4% of the cost a year and a 15-year life, as in the 2025 ATB's residential battery.

hp.note: EIA's air-source heat pumps, installed cost in 2022 dollars: the minimum-efficiency unit (HSPF 8.2, about COP 2.4 over the season) and the most efficient (HSPF 12.4, about COP 3.6). COP = HSPF ÷ 3.412. Illustrative: the heat pump is big enough for the coldest hour, its efficiency falls 3% for each °C colder, scaled so the season's average matches the rating, and it lasts 15 years. It replaces the gas furnace; a furnace's own replacement cost is not counted.

home.horizonNote: 25 years, the panels' life. The battery and the heat pump are bought again in year 15; at year 25 the second one still has a third of its life, counted as a residual value (straight line).

farm.label: Ridge wind farm

wind.note: Onshore wind: $1,712 per kW to build and $34.57 per kW a year to keep up (2025 dollars); 30 years. Output follows SPP's 2025 wind shape, month by month, with a 33.8% yearly capacity factor (the U.S. fleet in 2025); the best hours reach the farm's full size.

sale.note: Illustrative: a fixed contract at $50/MWh for every MWh sent to the grid (lesson A1's price), or a time-of-use contract at $40/MWh and $100/MWh from 16:00 to 21:00. The line to the grid carries at most its limit, and the farm only sells: it cannot buy power.

battery.note: EIA's four-hour lithium-ion battery: $1,521 per kW ($380 per kWh of storage) and $41.84 per kW a year (2025 dollars); 15% of the energy is lost in storage (85% round trip); 15-year life.

electrolyzer.note: DOE's PEM electrolyzer: about $2,000 per kW installed (2022 dollars); fixed upkeep 5% of that a year; 57.5 kWh of electricity per kg of hydrogen; 11% of the cost again for each 40,000 hours at full power (counted per MWh used); 30-year life.

tank.note: Illustrative: $800 per kg of hydrogen the tank can hold, 30-year life, no upkeep.

h2.note: Illustrative: hydrogen sold at a set price per kg to one buyer, who takes at most a set amount each hour. If it replaces hydrogen made from natural gas (0.18 MMBtu of gas per kg, feedstock and heat), each kg avoids 0.18 × 52.91 = 9.52 kg of CO2 at the plant.

farm.horizonNote: 30 years, the wind farm's life. A battery is bought again in year 15.

weeks.note: The engine runs representative weeks hour by hour, as lesson 13 and M3 do: for each season the week closest to all the others (a medoid), scaled to keep the season's energy, plus weeks kept as they are. Home: the week with the highest household use and the week with the highest need net of 6 kW of panels. Wind farm: the week with the least wind. Each week stands for its weeks of the year (weights). Batteries and the tank end each week where they started: storage from one week to the next is left out.

tie.note: Tie rule: a wear charge of 0.02¢ per kWh (home) or 2¢ per MWh (wind farm) on the energy into and out of the battery, so the battery never cycles for nothing. It is left out of every reported number. Several schedules can still tie hour by hour; the totals the bench reports are shared by every least-cost schedule (checked in the test).
